pages.title: Maximum demand and diversity
pages.for: The largest current the installation, or one board, draws at any one time. The supply and every submain are sized from it; Regulation 311.1 leaves the assessment to the designer.
pages.rule:
Lighting: I = W ÷ (230 × pf), fluorescent tube W × 1.25 first if no ballast loss is given
Neutral, same pf, no harmonics: IN = √(I1² + I2² + I3² − I1·I2 − I2·I3 − I3·I1)
Per phase, shared evenly: single-phase total after diversity ÷ 3, + each three-phase line current

Share single-phase circuits about equally over L1, L2 and L3: the heaviest phase sets the size.
Diversity: On-Site Guide Appendix A, guidance (slides p.10). None on EV points without load management: the course's choice, argued.

traps.text: Diversity treated as a rule: it is guidance and need not be applied.
Every single-phase circuit on one phase: the neutral carries the lot.
traps.cite: Slides p.33; IET EngX forum, in research (unbalanced currents do not cancel)

traps.text: Fluorescent tube watts alone: the ballast's loss is extra.
traps.cite: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide, fluorescent lamps, in research

traps.text: The motor's line current divided by three with the single-phase loads.
traps.cite: Slides p.13 (Ib of a three-phase load is a line current)

traps.text: Diversity on EV charge points without load management: the course takes none, though it is argued.
traps.cite: The IEC wording in the Schneider guide (factor 1 without load management); BS 7671 722.311.201 (NAPIT) is the regulation that lets load curtailment count; argued on the IET EngX forum, in research

Your slides p.10: the percentages are only found in the On-Site Guide, so they are guidance and do not have to be applied, and ten 100 W lamps could be designed at 660 W rather than 1000 W.

"BS 7671 sets them": it has no diversity table; the On-Site Guide gives the recognised figures.

"Wherever the On-Site Guide gives one": its figures, such as 66% for domestic lighting or 90% for a shop's lighting, may still be left off.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: [[Maximum demand]] is the largest current an installation draws at any one time. The supply and each submain are sized from it: Regulation 311.1 accepts it may be worked out for the whole installation or a part of it, so each board gets its own figure. Your assignment asks for it in question 10, "making informed assumptions where necessary", linked to question 1b's balancing.
pages.alt: If it is skipped or wrong: too low, and the supply fuse, or a submain's device and cable, carries more than it was chosen for (the course's reasoning); too high, and the cables are bigger and dearer than they need be (your slides p.10). A figure with diversity is an estimate, which the IET accepts may occasionally be exceeded.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A board's lighting circuits carry 10 A on L1, 10 A on L2 and 4 A on L3, at about the same power factor. What does the neutral carry?
pages.why: The 4 A on each phase cancels, leaving 6 A on L1 and 6 A on L2, a third of a cycle apart, whose sum is 6 A. By the rule: √(100 + 100 + 16 − 100 − 40 − 40) = √36 = 6.00 A.
pages.html: √(100 + 100 + 16 − 100 − 40 − 40) = √36 = 6.00 A

pages.name: Diversity
pages.text: Not every load runs flat out at once, so a building draws less than its connected load. Your slides call [[diversity]] designing with common sense rather than for the maximum (p.10).
pages.alt: The allowances this lesson uses, from the On-Site Guide's column for small shops, stores, offices and business premises. The course reads a showroom into that column, its own assumption; a training provider warns that commercial work may need measured loads instead. Lighting: 90% of the total current demand Heating and power: 100% of the largest appliance + 75% of the rest Motors: 100% of the largest + 80% of the second largest + 60% of the rest (the showroom has only one) Standard circuits: 100% of the largest circuit + 50% of every other Only these; read the rest in your copy.
pages.html:
The allowances this lesson uses, from the On-Site Guide's column for small shops, stores, offices and business premises. The course reads a showroom into that column, its own assumption; a training provider warns that commercial work may need measured loads instead.

  • Lighting: 90% of the total current demand
  • Heating and power: 100% of the largest appliance + 75% of the rest
  • Motors: 100% of the largest + 80% of the second largest + 60% of the rest (the showroom has only one)
  • Standard circuits: 100% of the largest circuit + 50% of every other

Only these; read the rest in your copy.

EV charge points: the IEC wording sets the factor at 1 unless a load management system is used. Regulation 722.311 lets load curtailment count, and your guide makes load management optional (p.9).

Where it's argued
  • On the IET forum, one contributor says BS 7671 does not prohibit diversity on EV points; another, that without load management it is still none.
  • Your slides apply 66% to one lighting circuit's Ib (p.10); a training provider applies diversity only to the total at the origin; an IET answer says it might only rarely be appropriate for one circuit.
  • The Schneider guide applies its factor to the loads on a board, and advises close to 1 for mainly lighting.

The course's choice: the lighting at 100%, because question 5a has the internal showroom lights on from 7.30 am to 9 pm (pack p.4), and the course takes the rest of the lighting with them. The On-Site Guide would allow 90%: a designer's call.

Sharing: the single-phase loads shared evenly over the three phases, ÷ 3, as an older book works a balanced line current.

Lighting: 24.35 + 38.74 = 63.09 A

Sockets: 32 + 0.5 × 7 × 32 = 32 + 112 = 144.00 A

Fixed points: 32 + 0.75 × 3 × 20 = 32 + 45 = 77.00 A

EV: 4 × 32 = 128.00 A

63.09 + 144.00 + 77.00 + 128.00 = 412.09 A; 412.09 ÷ 3 = 137.36 A; 137.36 + 23.08 = 160.44 A

About 160 A a phase: an estimate on practice values, as question 10 allows. A real split is heavier on one phase: four 32 A EV outlets cannot share evenly over three phases, so one phase carries two, 2 × 32 = 64 A, against an even share of 128 ÷ 3 = 42.67 A, unless other circuits move off it.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: State two reasons a designer applies diversity.
pages.why: A model answer: Not every load runs at full current at the same time, so designing for every load at once overstates what the installation draws; your slides call diversity designing with common sense rather than for the maximum (p.10). Allowing for it keeps cable sizes smaller and costs lower (p.10), and lets the supply, submains and switchgear be chosen for the maximum demand they will really carry. It is guidance from the On-Site Guide, applied with judgement, not a rule.
